research_question: Why has solar power become cheaper, and which cost components and uncertainties affect the trend?

sources.title: Documenting a Decade of Cost Declines for PV Systems
sources.reliability: U.S. national laboratory specializing in renewable energy
notes: NREL reported declines in residential, commercial-rooftop, and utility-scale PV system costs between 2010 and 2020.
Module efficiency and hardware and inverter costs contributed to lower system costs.
Soft costs remain a substantial part of residential and commercial installations.

sources.title: Learning a Better Way To Forecast Wind and Solar Energy Costs
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Energy Technologies Office
sources.reliability: Government energy agency summarizing Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory research
notes: Learning curves relate cost changes to cumulative deployment.
Levelized electricity cost depends on installed cost, financing, operations, and annual generation.
Historical learning rates vary over time; future projections carry uncertainty.

sources.title: Utility-Scale PV: 2024 Annual Technology Baseline
sources.reliability: National laboratory technology and cost benchmark
notes: PV cost scenarios depend on modules, inverters, installation, efficiency, and energy yield.
Projected cost reductions depend on assumptions and are not guaranteed outcomes.

sources.title: Soft Costs
notes: Soft costs include design, siting, permits, installation, interconnection, finance, customer acquisition, training, and overhead.
As hardware gets cheaper, non-hardware expenses make up a larger share of total installed cost.

sources.title: Solar Energy Evolution and Diffusion Studies
notes: PV costs have historically declined alongside cumulative production and deployment.
Technology progress combines manufacturing experience, research, and deployment.
